translations.text: In the days of Decius, the cruel emperor, the holy bishop Sixtus was living in the city of Rome. Then the emperor suddenly ordered that the bishop be brought before him [lit. "into his sight"; the text has "gesihum", probably for "gesihðum"] together with his priests.
Then Sixtus called out fearlessly to his priests: "My brothers, do not be afraid. Come, and let none of you fear the brief torments.
The holy martyrs suffered many torments so that they might come without care to the crown of glory of eternal life." Then his two deacons, Felicissimus and Agapitus, answered,
"You, our father, where shall we go without you?" That night the bishop and his two deacons were quickly brought to the cruel persecutor.
The emperor Decius said to him, "Offer your sacrifice to the immortal gods, and be the chief of the priests." The blessed Sixtus answered him,
"I have always offered, and still offer, my sacrifice to Almighty God, and to his Son, the Saviour Christ, and to the Holy Spirit: a pure and unblemished sacrifice."
Decius said, "Save yourself and your priests, and offer sacrifice. Truly, if you do not, you shall be an example to all others."
Sixtus truly answered, "A little while ago I told you that I always offer to Almighty God." Then Decius said to his soldiers,
"Lead him to the temple of Mars, so that he may offer to the god Mars. If he will not offer, shut him up in the Mamertine prison."
The soldiers led him to the idol and threatened him, telling him that he must offer his sacrifice to the dead image.
When he scorned the emperor's command and would not offer to the idol, they put him, with his two deacons, into the dark prison.
Meanwhile Laurence, his archdeacon, came and spoke to the holy bishop with these words:
"You, my father, where are you journeying without your son? You holy priest, where are you hastening without your deacon?
It was not your custom to offer to God without your deacon. What has displeased you in me, my father?"
Show your power in your son, and offer to God the one whom you have trained, so that you may come all the more securely to the noble crown of glory."
When the blessed Laurence lamented with these and many other words that he was not allowed to suffer with his teacher, the bishop answered,
"My son, I am not forsaking you; rather, a greater warfare befits you in your struggle."
We, as old men, undertake the short course of a lighter struggle; but you, being young, will win a much more glorious victory over this cruel king.
My child, stop your weeping: after three days you will come to me victorious into eternal life. Now take the treasures of our church and distribute them to Christian people, as seems good to you."
Then Laurence the archdeacon went, as the bishop had commanded, and distributed the church's treasures to priests, to poor strangers, and to widows, to each according to his need.
He came to a certain widow named Cyriaca, who had hidden priests and many lay Christians in her home.
Then the blessed Laurence washed the feet of all of them, and healed the widow of a grievous headache.
Also a blind man fell weeping at his feet, asking to be healed. Then Laurence marked the sign of the cross on the blind man's eyes, and he at once saw clearly.
The archdeacon then found out about more Christians in various places, and before his martyrdom he visited them with spiritual peace and with the washing of feet.
When he had returned from there, his teacher Sixtus had been led out of the prison with his two deacons before the emperor Decius.
The emperor then grew enraged against the holy bishop, saying, "Indeed, we are sparing you because of your age: obey our commands and offer to the immortal gods."
The blessed bishop answered him, "You wretch, spare yourself, and do penance for the blood of the saints that you have shed."
The bloodthirsty murderer, with an angry mind, said to his chief prefect, Valerian,
"If this bold-spoken bishop is not killed, the fear of us will no longer be dreaded." Valerian answered him, "Let him be beheaded."
Have them led back to the temple of the god Mars, and if they will not pray to him on bent knees and offer their sacrifice, let them suffer beheading in that same place."
The emperor's soldiers led him to the idol-temple with his two deacons. Then the bishop looked toward the temple and said,
"You dumb idol, through you wretched people lose eternal life. May the almighty Son of God overthrow you."
Then at that word part of the temple burst apart and fell suddenly. Laurence then cried out to the bishop,
"Holy father, do not forsake me, for I have spent the church's treasures as you commanded me."
Then the soldiers seized him, because they had heard him speak about the church's treasures.
Then Sixtus truly bowed beneath the sword's edge, and his two deacons with him, Felicissimus and Agapitus, in front of the temple, on the sixth day of this month.
Afterwards Laurence was brought to the emperor, and the cruel murderer asked him, "Where are the church's treasures that were entrusted to you?"
The blessed Laurence answered him not a word. On the same day the enemy of God handed the holy deacon over to his chief prefect Valerian with this command:
"Exact the treasures diligently, and bend him to the immortal gods." The prefect then handed him over to his subordinate, whose name was Hippolytus, and he shut him up in prison with many others.
There in the prison he found a heathen man who had been blinded by much weeping. Then he said to him,
"Lucillus, if you believe in the Saviour Christ, he will give light to your eyes." He answered, "I have always wished to be baptized in Christ's name."
Laurence said to him, "Do you believe with all your heart?" He answered, weeping, "I believe in the Saviour Christ, and I renounce the false idols."
Hippolytus listened patiently to their words. The blessed Lawrence then taught the blind man the true faith of the Holy Trinity, and baptized him.
After his baptism Lucillus cried out in a clear voice, "Blessed be the eternal God, the Saviour Christ, who has given me light through his deacon.

"I was blind in both eyes; now I enjoy the light brightly." Then indeed many other blind people came weeping to the blessed deacon, and he laid his hands over their eyes, and they received their sight.
Then the town prefect Hippolytus said to the deacon, "Reveal the church's treasures to me." Laurence said,
"O Hippolytus, if you believe in God the Father and in his Son, the Saviour Christ, I will reveal the treasures to you and promise you eternal life."
Hippolytus said, "If you fulfil these words with deeds, then I will do as you direct me." Lawrence then blessed a font and baptized him.
Indeed, after the bath of baptism Hippolytus was crying out with a clear voice, "I have seen the souls of innocent people rejoicing in God."
And with tears he said to the blessed deacon, "I beseech you in the Saviour's name that all my household may be baptized."
Laurence gladly granted him this, and with glory baptized nineteen men and women of his household.
After this the chief prefect sent word and commanded Hippolytus to bring Lawrence to the king's palace.
Hippolytus made the command known to the blessed Lawrence in humble speech. He said, "Let us go, for glory is prepared for me and for you."
Then they came quickly and stood before him unafraid. Then Valerian said to the holy martyr, "Now cast off your obstinacy, and give up the treasures."
God's witness answered him, "I have spent them on God's poor, and they are the eternal treasures that will never be diminished." The prefect said,
"Why do you play with words? Offer your sacrifice to our gods, and give up the sorcery that you trust in."
Lawrence said, "Why does the devil compel you to threaten Christian people into his worship?
If it is right that we should pray to devils rather than to Almighty God, then you judge who is worthy of that honour: the one who was made, or the one who created all things."
Then the emperor answered, "What is that which is made, or what is he who made it?" God's witness said,
"The Almighty Father of our Saviour is the Creator of all creatures, and you say that I must pray to dumb stones, which are carved by men's hands."
Then the emperor grew angry. He ordered the deacon to be stripped in front of him and cruelly scourged, and the emperor himself cried out, "Do not insult our gods."
In the middle of the torments the blessed Lawrence said, "Truly I thank my God, who has judged me worthy to be among his saints. And you, wretch, are tormented in your own madness."
Decius said to the executioners, "Raise him up, and show him all the instruments of torture."
Then iron plates, iron claws, an iron bed, lead-weighted whips and other spiked whips were quickly brought out. Then the emperor said,
"Offer your sacrifice to our gods, or you will be tortured with all these instruments of torment." The blessed deacon said,
"You wretched man, I have always longed for these delicacies: they will be to my glory and to your punishment." The emperor said,
"Reveal to us all the wicked people like you, so that this city may be cleansed; and offer to our gods yourself, and do not trust at all in your gold-hoards."
Then the holy martyr said, "Truly I do trust, and I am free from care about my hoards." Decius answered,
"Do you think that you will be set free from these torments by your hoards?" and then in a fierce mood he ordered the executioners to beat him with stout clubs.
Lawrence, however, cried out during the beating, "You wretch, understand at least now that I am victorious through Christ's treasures, and I do not feel your torments at all."
Decius said, "Lay the iron plates, glowing hot, against his sides." The blessed martyr then prayed to his Lord, and said,

"Saviour Christ, God from God, have mercy on your servant, because when I was accused I did not deny you; when I was questioned I confessed you." Then the emperor ordered him to be raised up, and said,
"I see that through your sorcery you make a mockery of these torments; but you shall not make a mockery of me.
I swear by all the gods and goddesses that you shall sacrifice, or I will kill you with various tortures." Then Lawrence boldly cried out,
"In my Lord's name I am not at all afraid of your torments, which are transitory: do not stop what you have begun."
Then the emperor became enraged with violent fury, and ordered the holy deacon to be flogged for a long time with lead-weighted whips. Then Lawrence cried out,
"Saviour Christ, you who deigned to be born as a human being and redeemed us from the devil's slavery, receive my spirit."
At that same moment an answer came to him from heaven, saying, "You must still endure much struggle in your martyrdom." Then Decius cried out in fury,
"Men of Rome, did you hear the devils' comfort given to this sacrilegious man, who fears neither our angered gods nor the torments we have devised?
Stretch him out, and torment him by flogging him with spiked whips." Then Lawrence, stretched out on the rack, thanked his Lord with a smiling mouth:
"Lord God, Father of the Saviour Christ, may you be blessed, who have granted us your mercy;
show your kindness now, so that these bystanders may know that you comfort your servants."
At that moment one of the soldiers, whose name was Romanus, believed, and said to God's witness,
"Laurence, I see an angel of God standing before you with a towel, wiping your sweating limbs. Now I beg you, by God, do not forsake me."
Then Decius was filled with malice, and said to his prefect, "It seems to me that we are being overcome by sorcery."
Then he ordered the deacon to be released from the rack and handed over to the town reeve Hippolytus. He did not yet know that he was a Christian.
Meanwhile the believing soldier Romanus brought a pitcher of water. Weeping, he went to the feet of holy Lawrence and asked to be baptized.
Laurence quickly blessed the water and baptized the faithful retainer. When Decius found out, he ordered him stripped of his clothes and beaten with stout clubs.
Then Romanus, without being asked, cried out in the emperor's presence, "I am a Christian." At that very moment the cruel murderer ordered him put to the sword.
Later that same night, after the soldier's martyrdom, Decius went to the hot baths near the palace of Sallust and ordered holy Lawrence to be brought to him.
Then Hippolytus began to lament bitterly, and said, "I want to go with you, and cry out in a loud voice that I am a Christian, and lie dead with you." Laurence said,
"Do not weep; rather, be silent and rejoice, because I am going to God's glory. In a little while, when I call you, hear my voice and come to me."
Then Decius ordered all the instruments of torture to be made ready before his judgment seat, and Laurence was brought to him. Decius said,
"Give up your trust in your sorcery, and tell us your family." The blessed Laurence answered,
"By human birth I am Spanish, a foster-child of Rome, and a Christian from the cradle, brought up in all of God's law." Decius answered,
"Truly that law is divine which has made you so bold that you will not worship our gods and do not fear any kind of torment."
Laurence said, "In Christ's name I am not afraid of your torments." Then the cruel emperor said,
"If you do not sacrifice to our gods, this whole night shall be spent on you with various tortures." Laurence said,
"My night has no darkness; it shines with bright light." Then the cruel man ordered the saint's mouth to be struck with stones.
Then Laurence was strengthened through God's grace, and said with a laughing mouth, "Praise be to you, Lord, for you are the God of all things."
Decius said to the executioners, "Lift the iron bed onto the fire, so that the proud Laurence may rest himself on it."
At once they stripped him of his clothes, stretched him out on the hard bed, packed the space under the bed with burning coals, and pressed him down from above with iron forks.
Then Decius said to God's martyr, "Sacrifice to our gods now." Laurence answered,
"I offer myself to Almighty God as a sweet-smelling fragrance, because a troubled spirit is a sacrifice acceptable to God."
The executioners kept raking the coals under the bed, and from above they pressed him down with their forks. Then Laurence said,
"O you wretched men, do you not see that your coals give my body no heat, but rather coolness?"
Then again, with the most radiant face, he said, "Saviour Christ, I thank you that you will strengthen me."
Then he looked toward the emperor and said, "Look, you wretch, you have roasted one side of my body. Now turn the other, and eat." Then he spoke again:
"Saviour Christ, I thank you with all my heart that I may go into your kingdom."
And with these words he gave up his spirit, and by such a martyrdom went to the heavenly kingdom, in which he dwells with God forever in eternity.
Then the cruel emperor left the holy body on the iron grid, and hurried with his chief prefect to the Tiberian palace.
Then Hippolytus buried the holy body with great reverence in the burial place of the widow Cyriaca, on this present day.
Indeed, a great multitude of Christian people kept vigil at the tomb with intense lamentation. The holy priest Justin then said mass for them all and gave them communion.
After this Hippolytus returned to his home, kissed his household with God's peace, and gave them all communion.
Then suddenly, as he sat down, the emperor's soldiers came, seized him, and led him to the executioner.
Then Decius asked him with a smirk, "Well now, have you turned into a sorcerer, since you buried Laurence?" He answered,
"I did it not as a sorcerer but as a Christian." Then Decius grew angry and ordered his mouth to be struck with stones and his clothes to be stripped off him, and said,
"What, were you not a devoted worshipper of our gods? And now you have become so foolish that you are not even ashamed of your nakedness."
Hippolytus answered, "I was foolish, and now I am wise and a Christian. In my ignorance I believed in the error that you believe in."
Decius said, "Sacrifice to the gods, or you will perish under torture, as Laurence did." He answered,
"Oh, if only I could follow the example of the blessed Laurence!" Decius said, "Stretch him out naked as he is, and beat him with stiff rods."
When he had been beaten for a long time, he thanked God. Decius said, "Hippolytus mocks your rods; beat him with spiked scourges."
They did so until they grew weary. Hippolytus cried out with a loud voice, "I am a Christian."
So the cruel emperor, when he could not lure him away from the faith of Christ with any tortures, commanded his chief prefect to kill him with a cruel death.
On the same day Valerian searched through his possessions, and found nineteen men and women of his household who had been baptized at the hands of the blessed Lawrence.
To them Valerian said, "Consider your age, and save your lives, lest you perish together with your lord Hippolytus."
Then they answered with one mind, "We would rather die purely with our lord than live impurely with you."
Then Valerian became furious, and ordered Hippolytus to be led out of the city with his household. Then the blessed Hippolytus encouraged his household, and said,
"My brothers, do not be sad or afraid, because you and I have one Lord, God Almighty."

Then Valerian commanded all his household to be beheaded in Hippolytus's sight, and commanded him himself to be tied by the feet to the necks of untamed horses, and so dragged through thorns and brambles;
and with that dragging he gave up his spirit on the thirteenth day of this month. On the same night the holy Justin gathered the bodies of them all and buried them.
Then, after the passion of these saints, Decius rode in a golden chariot, together with Valerian, to their heathen temple, so that they might force the Christians to their wicked sacrifices.
Then Decius was suddenly driven mad by a fiendish spirit, and cried out, "O you, Hippolytus, where are you dragging me, bound with sharp chains?"
Valerian also, gone mad, cried out, "O you, Laurence, harshly you drag me, bound with burning chains." And he died on the spot.
Indeed, Decius went terribly mad, and for three days he cried out continually with a devilish voice, "I beseech you, Lawrence, let up somewhat on the torments."

Lo, then great lamentation and bitter weeping arose in the household, and the emperor's wife ordered all the Christians who were in prison to be led out; and on the third day Decius died in great torments.
Truly, Queen Triphonia sought the feet of the holy priest Justin with bitter tears, and her daughter Cyrilla together with her, asking for holy baptism.
Justin then received them with great joy, and enjoined on them a fast of seven days, and afterwards washed them with the holy bath of baptism from all their wicked deeds.

When the emperor's thegns heard that Queen Triphonia and Decius's daughter Cyrilla had turned to the faith of Christ and to saving baptism, they then sought out the holy priest together with their wives, and asked for mercy and baptism.
When these things had happened, the blessed Justin consulted with the Christians about whom they wanted to choose as bishop in the see of Sixtus.
They then unanimously chose a venerable man whose name was Dionysius, whom Bishop Maximus of the city of Ostia consecrated to the Roman episcopal see with honour.
Let us now pray with humble voice to the holy martyr of God, Laurence, whose feast-day this present day makes known to the whole faithful Church,
that he may intercede for us with the Heavenly King, for whose name he suffered many torments with a bold mind, and with whom he rejoices in glory, free from care, for eternity. Amen.
